problem_statements.problem_statement: How many policies are in the portfolio?
problem_statements.business_intent: Establish the size of the book.
problem_statements.business_objective: Give the executive the single headline volume figure.
example_queries: What is the total policy count?
How many applications do we have?
analytical_steps: Load Policy_Details.
Count distinct AppID values.
Report the count.
problem_statements.answer_template: The portfolio contains {policy_count} policies.
problem_statements.population: All rows in Policy_Details (one row per policy application).
problem_statements.caveat: The five CSVs are a single point-in-time extract. Figures describe the portfolio as extracted, not a live book.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All rows in Policy_Details (one row per policy application).

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the distribution of policies across policy statuses?
problem_statements.business_intent: Show the health mix of the book at a glance.
problem_statements.business_objective: Quantify how the portfolio splits across in-force, lapsed, surrendered and death.
example_queries: What is the policy status split?
How many policies are lapsed, surrendered or in force?
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by POLICY.STATUS.
Count policies per status.
Compute each status share of the total.
Order by count descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: Of {policy_count} policies, {top_status} accounts for {top_share}%.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: POLICY.STATUS has exactly four values; no other lifecycle state exists in the data.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the total annualised premium equivalent (APE) of the portfolio?
problem_statements.business_intent: Quantify the premium scale of the book.
problem_statements.business_objective: Report total APE as the headline revenue-proxy measure.
example_queries: How much premium does the book represent?
analytical_steps: Load Policy_Details.
Sum the APE column across all policies.
Report the total.
problem_statements.answer_template: Total portfolio APE is {total_ape}.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies; APE is fully populated with no nulls.
problem_statements.caveat: APE is an annualised premium measure, not collected cash. No payment data exists.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies; APE is fully populated with no nulls.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the total sum assured exposure of the portfolio?
problem_statements.business_intent: Quantify gross risk exposure.
problem_statements.business_objective: Report total sum assured as the headline exposure measure.
example_queries: How much cover have we written?
analytical_steps: Load Policy_Details.
Sum Sum.Assured across all policies.
Report the total.
problem_statements.answer_template: Total sum assured exposure is {total_sum_assured}.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies; Sum.Assured is fully populated with no nulls.
problem_statements.caveat: Gross exposure before any reinsurance; no reinsurance data exists in the CSVs.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies; Sum.Assured is fully populated with no nulls.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the average and median APE per policy?
problem_statements.business_intent: Understand typical policy value.
problem_statements.business_objective: Report central tendency of APE, using median alongside mean because APE is skewed.
example_queries: What is the average policy size?
analytical_steps: Load Policy_Details.
Compute mean APE.
Compute median APE.
Report both and note the gap as a skew indicator.
problem_statements.answer_template: Average APE is {avg_ape} and median APE is {median_ape} across {policy_count} policies.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: APE ranges from 6,000 to 2,500,000; the mean is pulled upward by large cases, so the median is the better typical value.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the split between traditional and ULIP policies?
problem_statements.business_intent: Show the product-class mix of the book.
problem_statements.business_objective: Quantify traditional versus unit-linked composition by volume and premium.
example_queries: How many ULIP policies do we have?
What share of the book is unit linked?
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by Trad.ULIP.
Count policies and sum APE per class.
Compute each class share of policies and of APE.
Report both views.
problem_statements.answer_template: ULIP accounts for {ulip_share}% of policies and a differing share of APE.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies; Trad.ULIP has exactly two values, TRAD and ULIP.
problem_statements.caveat: Trad.ULIP maps deterministically onto Prod_No; ULIP is a single product (P56).

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies; Trad.ULIP has exactly two values, TRAD and ULIP.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How many policies does each product account for?
problem_statements.business_intent: Show which products carry the book.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank the ten products by policy volume and share.
example_queries: How is the book split across products?
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by Prod_No and Plan.Name.
Count policies per product.
Compute share of portfolio.
Order by count descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {top_product} leads with {top_count} policies ({top_share}% of the book).
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies, spread across the 10 products.
problem_statements.caveat: Prod_No maps one-to-one onto Plan.Name; the two are interchangeable labels.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies, spread across the 10 products.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which products contribute the most APE?
problem_statements.business_intent: Identify the premium engines of the book.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank products by total APE and contrast with volume rank.
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by product.
Sum APE and count policies per product.
Compute average APE per policy per product.
Compute each product share of total APE.
Rank by total APE descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {top_product} contributes {top_share}% of total APE from {top_count} policies.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies grouped by product.
problem_statements.caveat: Volume rank and APE rank can differ; a low-volume product with high average APE can outrank a high-volume one.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies grouped by product.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Give me an executive snapshot of portfolio health.
problem_statements.business_intent: One-screen portfolio status for leadership.
problem_statements.business_objective: Combine volume, premium, exposure, status mix and retention into a single briefing.
analytical_steps: Count policies and sum APE and Sum.Assured.
Compute the status mix and derive in-force, lapse and surrender rates.
Join Persistency on AppID and compute the renewal paid rate over the eligible population.
Count distinct products.
Assemble the metrics into one KPI table.
State which figures are snapshot measures and which are rates.
problem_statements.answer_template: Portfolio: {policy_count} policies, {total_ape} APE, {total_sum_assured} sum assured. In-force {inforce_rate}%, lapsed {lapse_rate}%, surrendered {surrender_rate}%. Renewal paid rate {renewal_paid_rate}%.
problem_statements.population: Policy metrics over all policies; renewal metrics over the 24,542 active-or-lapsed policies present in Persistency_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: Renewal and policy metrics use different denominators: Persistency excludes surrendered and death policies by design (DQ-006). The five CSVs are a single point-in-time extract. Figures describe the portfolio as extracted, not a live book.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: stated per metric

problem_statements.problem_statement: How many distinct agents, branches and clients does the portfolio involve?
problem_statements.business_intent: Size the distribution and customer base.
problem_statements.business_objective: Report the distinct entity counts underpinning the book.
example_queries: How many agents do we have?
analytical_steps: Count distinct SALES_ID and Branch_No in Policy_Details.
Join Owner_Details on AppID and count distinct ClientID.
Report all three counts and note that clients are fewer than policies.
problem_statements.answer_template: {agent_count} agents across {branch_count} branches serve {client_count} distinct clients.
problem_statements.population: All policies, joined to owners on AppID.
problem_statements.caveat: ClientID repeats: 237 clients hold more than one policy (max 3), so clients are fewer than policies.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies, joined to owners on AppID.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What proportion of the portfolio is still actively paying premium?
problem_statements.business_intent: Measure the healthy, revenue-generating share of the book.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute the in-force rate as a headline retention indicator.
example_queries: What percentage of policies are in force?
How much of the book is still paying?
analytical_steps: Count policies with POLICY.STATUS = 'Premium paying (regular)'.
Divide by total policy count.
Express as a percentage.
problem_statements.answer_template: {inforce_rate}% of the {policy_count} policies are premium paying.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: 'Premium paying (regular)' is the only in-force state present; there is no paid-up or reduced-paid-up state in the data.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the distribution of policy terms across the book?
problem_statements.business_intent: Understand contract duration structure.
problem_statements.business_objective: Show how policy term is distributed and identify the dominant terms.
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by Policy.Term.
Count policies per term.
Compute share and cumulative share.
Report the dominant terms and the range.
problem_statements.answer_template: Policy terms range from {min_term} to {max_term} years; {top_term} years is most common at {top_share}%.
problem_statements.population: All policies; Policy.Term is fully populated with 43 distinct values.
problem_statements.caveat: Policy.Term is the contractual term, not elapsed duration. Elapsed tenure must be derived from Inforce.Date.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies; Policy.Term is fully populated with 43 distinct values.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which product has the highest lapse rate?
problem_statements.business_intent: Find the product losing the most customers proportionally.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank products by lapse rate and identify the worst performer with its peer context.
example_queries: Which plan has the most lapses?

baseline.description: portfolio lapse rate across all policies

analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by product.
Count total policies and lapsed policies per product.
Compute lapse rate per product.
Compute the portfolio lapse rate as the baseline.
Flag products with fewer than 50 policies as low-sample.
Rank by lapse rate descending and report the leader against the baseline.
problem_statements.answer_template: {worst_product} has the highest lapse rate at {worst_rate}% versus a portfolio average of {baseline_rate}%.
problem_statements.population: All policies, grouped by product.
problem_statements.caveat: Lapse is read from POLICY.STATUS = 'Lapsed'. There is no lapse-date column, so a lapse cannot be attributed to a period. Product P18 has only 11 policies, so its rate is statistically unstable and is flagged rather than ranked.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies, grouped by product.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Why does the worst-performing product have such a high lapse rate?
problem_statements.business_intent: Explain a product lapse outlier using only observable differences.
problem_statements.business_objective: Identify which observable attributes of the worst product differ materially from peers, without asserting causation.
example_queries: Why does this product lapse so much?
What is driving lapses in that plan?
What makes this product lapse more than others?
analytical_steps: Identify the product with the highest lapse rate.
Define the peer set as all other products with at least 50 policies.
Join Owner_Details and Sales_Details to enrich each policy.
For the target and the peer set, compute average APE, sum assured, term, premium paying term, owner age, owner income and selling-agent first-year persistency.
Compute the difference and percentage difference for each attribute.
Rank attributes by absolute percentage difference to surface the largest observable gaps.
Report only differences the data establishes, and state explicitly that association is not proof of cause.
problem_statements.answer_template: {target_product} lapses at {target_rate}% versus {peer_rate}% for peers. The largest observable differences are {top_drivers}. These are associations, not proven causes.
problem_statements.population: The target product versus all other products with at least 50 policies.
problem_statements.caveat: The dataset contains no lapse reason, no payment history and no customer contact record, so the mechanism of lapse cannot be established. Only attribute differences between lapsing and non-lapsing populations are observable.

calculations: delta and pct delta per attribute
evidence_requirements.population_definition: The target product versus all other products with at least 50 policies.

limitations: Cannot establish causation; reports observable association only.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the average sum assured by product?
problem_statements.business_intent: Compare the cover level each product delivers.
problem_statements.business_objective: Report mean and median sum assured per product.
example_queries: Which product gives the most cover?
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by product.
Compute mean and median Sum.Assured per product.
Include policy count for context.
Order by average descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {top_product} carries the highest average sum assured at {top_avg}.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies grouped by product.
problem_statements.caveat: Sum assured ranges from 14,000 to 28,708,128; medians are reported because the mean is skewed by large cases.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies grouped by product.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How do traditional and ULIP policies compare across key metrics?
problem_statements.business_intent: Contrast the two product classes on the measures that matter.
problem_statements.business_objective: Produce a side-by-side metric table for TRAD versus ULIP.
example_queries: How do unit linked policies differ?
Which performs better, TRAD or ULIP?

baseline.description: portfolio lapse rate across all policies

analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by Trad.ULIP.
For each class compute policy count, total and average APE, average sum assured, average term and lapse rate.
Compute the difference between the two classes for each metric.
Present as a side-by-side comparison table.
problem_statements.answer_template: ULIP: {ulip_count} policies at {ulip_lapse}% lapse. TRAD: {trad_count} policies at {trad_lapse}% lapse.
problem_statements.population: All policies split by Trad.ULIP.
problem_statements.caveat: ULIP comprises a single product (P56), so this comparison is partly a single-product comparison rather than a like-for-like class comparison.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies split by Trad.ULIP.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which products have the best customer retention?
problem_statements.business_intent: Identify products that keep customers.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank products by in-force rate, the inverse view of lapse.
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by product.
Compute in-force, lapse and surrender rates per product.
Flag products with fewer than 50 policies.
Rank by in-force rate descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {best_product} retains best with {best_rate}% still premium paying.
problem_statements.population: All policies, grouped by product, with low-sample products flagged.
problem_statements.caveat: Retention here is a snapshot status share, not a time-based persistency measure. Products sold more recently have had less time to lapse.

limitations: no vintage adjustment possible from status alone
evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies, grouped by product, with low-sample products flagged.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the average premium paying term by product?
problem_statements.business_intent: Understand the commitment length each product asks of customers.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compare premium paying term across products.
example_queries: Average premium paying term per product
How long do customers pay by product?
Which product has the longest paying term?
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by product.
Compute average and median PREMIUM.PAYING.TERM and Policy.Term.
Report both so limited-pay structures are visible.
Order by average premium paying term.
problem_statements.answer_template: {top_product} has the longest average premium paying term at {top_ppt} years.
problem_statements.population: All policies; both term columns are fully populated.
problem_statements.caveat: Where premium paying term is shorter than policy term the product is limited-pay; the data does not label this explicitly.

aggregates: avg PPT and term by product
evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies; both term columns are fully populated.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How concentrated is the portfolio across products?
problem_statements.business_intent: Assess product concentration risk.
problem_statements.business_objective: Quantify how much of the book depends on the top products.
example_queries: How concentrated is the product mix?
What share do the top 3 products hold?
Is the book too dependent on one product?
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by product and count policies and APE.
Sort products by share descending.
Compute the cumulative share of the top 1, top 3 and top 5 products.
Compute a Herfindahl-style concentration index from the shares.
Report both volume and APE concentration.
problem_statements.answer_template: The top 3 products hold {top3_share}% of policies and {top3_ape_share}% of APE.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies distributed across the 10 products.
problem_statements.caveat: Concentration is measured on a 10-product book; the index is not comparable to industry benchmarks without the same product granularity.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies distributed across the 10 products.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Give me a full performance scorecard for every product.
problem_statements.business_intent: One table that ranks every product on every available dimension.
problem_statements.business_objective: Build a multi-metric product scorecard combining volume, value, retention and claims.
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by product for volume, APE and status rates.
Left join Claims on AppID and compute claim incidence per product.
Left join Persistency on AppID and compute the renewal paid rate per product over the eligible population only.
Assemble all metrics into one row per product.
Flag products below the 50-policy sample threshold.
Rank products and present the scorecard.
problem_statements.answer_template: Product scorecard across {product_count} products; {best_product} leads on retention, {worst_product} on lapse.
problem_statements.population: All policies for volume and status metrics; the Persistency-eligible subset for renewal metrics; all claims for incidence.
problem_statements.caveat: Renewal metrics use a different denominator from status metrics because Persistency excludes surrendered and death policies (DQ-006). Claim incidence is based on 134 claims across 25,000 policies, so per-product claim rates are small-sample.

evidence_requirements.sample_sizes: policy and claim counts per product
limitations: claim rates are small-sample per product
evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies for volume and status metrics; the Persistency-eligible subset for renewal metrics; all claims for incidence.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which products show the widest gap between sum assured and premium?
problem_statements.business_intent: Identify which products deliver the most cover per premium rupee.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute the sum assured to APE multiple per product and rank it.
example_queries: Which product gives most cover per premium?
Sum assured to premium ratio by product
Which plan has the highest sum assured multiple?
analytical_steps: Derive sum_assured_multiple as Sum.Assured divided by APE for each policy.
Guard against zero or null APE before dividing.
Group by product and compute the median multiple, which resists outliers.
Rank products by median multiple descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {top_product} delivers the highest cover multiple at {top_multiple}x premium.
problem_statements.population: All policies with non-zero APE; APE has no zeros in this dataset so all 25,000 qualify.
problem_statements.caveat: The multiple is a structural product feature, not a measure of customer value or profitability. No cost or margin data exists.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies with non-zero APE; APE has no zeros in this dataset so all 25,000 qualify.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What does the APE distribution look like across the portfolio?
problem_statements.business_intent: Understand the spread and skew of policy premium.
problem_statements.business_objective: Bucket APE and report the distribution with percentiles.
example_queries: How is premium spread across policies?
What is the spread of premiums?
analytical_steps: Bucket APE into bands.
Count policies per band and compute each band share.
Compute the 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th and 99th percentiles.
Report the distribution shape and the mean-median gap.
problem_statements.answer_template: APE runs from {min_ape} to {max_ape}; the median is {median_ape} and the 90th percentile {p90_ape}.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: APE is strongly right-skewed, so band widths are reported explicitly and the mean is not used as the typical value.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which are the highest-value policies in the book?
problem_statements.business_intent: Surface the largest cases for relationship management.
problem_statements.business_objective: List the top N policies by APE with their key attributes.
analytical_steps: Sort Policy_Details by APE descending.
Take the top N, defaulting to 10.
Return AppID, APE, sum assured, plan, status and selling agent.
Report the combined share of the top N.
problem_statements.answer_template: The top {n} policies by APE total {topn_ape}, or {topn_share}% of portfolio APE.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details, ranked by APE descending.
problem_statements.caveat: AppID is a policy identifier. Owner names are available but are personal data and are excluded from this output by default.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details, ranked by APE descending.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How concentrated is premium among the largest policies?
problem_statements.business_intent: Assess dependence on a small number of large cases.
problem_statements.business_objective: Measure what share of APE the top percentile of policies represents.
example_queries: What share of APE comes from the top 1%?
Are we dependent on a few big policies?
How much premium sits in the largest cases?
analytical_steps: Sort policies by APE descending.
Compute cumulative APE.
Determine the APE share held by the top 1%, 5%, 10% and 20% of policies.
Report the concentration curve points.
problem_statements.answer_template: The top 1% of policies hold {top1_share}% of APE; the top 10% hold {top10_share}%.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details, ordered by APE descending.
problem_statements.caveat: Concentration is measured on APE, not on collected premium or profit, neither of which exists in the data.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details, ordered by APE descending.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Are there policies with anomalous premium relative to their cover?
problem_statements.business_intent: Surface cases whose pricing structure looks unusual.
problem_statements.business_objective: Flag policies whose sum assured to APE multiple is a statistical outlier within their product.
example_queries: Find policies with an unusual cover multiple
Outliers in sum assured to premium
analytical_steps: Derive the sum assured to APE multiple per policy.
Within each product compute the first and third quartile and the interquartile range.
Flag policies outside 1.5 times the IQR from the quartiles as outliers.
Compare within product rather than across, because products differ structurally.
Return the flagged policies with their product median for context.
problem_statements.answer_template: {outlier_count} policies fall outside the expected cover multiple range for their product.
problem_statements.population: All policies, assessed within their own product group.
problem_statements.caveat: An outlier is a statistical flag, not evidence of an error or of mis-selling. The data contains no underwriting or pricing rules against which to verify correctness.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies, assessed within their own product group.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the average APE by policy term band?
problem_statements.business_intent: See whether longer contracts carry larger premiums.
problem_statements.business_objective: Relate policy term to average premium.
example_queries: Average premium for long term policies
analytical_steps: Band Policy.Term into ranges.
Group policies by band.
Compute average and median APE and average sum assured per band.
Report the trend across bands with policy counts.
problem_statements.answer_template: Average APE by term band ranges from {min_band_ape} to {max_band_ape}.
problem_statements.population: All policies, banded by contractual policy term.
problem_statements.caveat: An association between term and premium is descriptive only; product design drives both, and product is a confounding factor.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies, banded by contractual policy term.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the total and average renewal premium due?
problem_statements.business_intent: Size the renewal premium opportunity.
problem_statements.business_objective: Report total and average renewal premium across the persistency population.
example_queries: How much renewal premium is due?
What is the renewal book worth?
analytical_steps: Load Persistency_Details.
Sum Renewal_Premium_Amount across all rows.
Compute average and median.
Report totals with the row count.
problem_statements.answer_template: Total renewal premium due is {total_renewal_premium} across {renewal_count} policies.
problem_statements.population: The 24,542 policies present in Persistency_Details (active or lapsed only).
problem_statements.caveat: This is premium due as recorded, covering only the persistency-eligible population; surrendered and death policies are excluded (DQ-006).

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 24,542 policies present in Persistency_Details (active or lapsed only).

problem_statements.problem_statement: How does renewal premium compare to original APE?
problem_statements.business_intent: Check whether renewal amounts track the original premium.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compare Renewal_Premium_Amount against policy APE on the joined population.
example_queries: Is renewal premium the same as APE?
Compare renewal amount to original premium
Do renewal premiums match the original?
analytical_steps: Join Policy_Details to Persistency_Details on AppID.
For each joined policy compute the difference between Renewal_Premium_Amount and APE.
Count exact matches, higher and lower cases.
Report the distribution of differences and the match rate.
problem_statements.answer_template: Renewal premium matches APE for {match_count} of {policy_count} joined policies.
problem_statements.population: The 24,541 policies present in both Policy_Details and Persistency_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: One policy cannot be joined because of the corrupted AppID (DQ-001) and is excluded from the comparison.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 24,541 policies present in both Policy_Details and Persistency_Details.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How long does it take for a policy to go from login to in-force?
problem_statements.business_intent: Measure new-business processing speed.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute underwriting turnaround as the gap between Login.Date and Inforce.Date.
example_queries: What is our underwriting turnaround time?
How long to issue a policy?
Average days from login to inforce
analytical_steps: Parse Login.Date and Inforce.Date using the contract's month-first format list.
Derive underwriting_days as Inforce.Date minus Login.Date.
Exclude any negative durations and report how many were excluded.
Compute mean, median, minimum and maximum turnaround.
problem_statements.answer_template: Median underwriting turnaround is {median_days} days (mean {avg_days}).
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies; both dates parse fully under the contract.
problem_statements.caveat: Policy dates mix '/' and '-' separators and are month-first; the parse contract in config/data_contract.json is applied (DQ-002). One policy has Login.Date after Inforce.Date (DQ-011) and is excluded from the duration statistics.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies; both dates parse fully under the contract.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which products are slowest to issue?
problem_statements.business_intent: Locate processing bottlenecks by product.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank products by median underwriting turnaround.
example_queries: Which product takes longest to issue?
Slowest products to go in force
analytical_steps: Derive underwriting_days per policy.
Group by product and compute median and mean turnaround.
Compute the portfolio median as the baseline.
Flag products with fewer than 50 policies.
Rank by median turnaround descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {slowest_product} is slowest at a median {slowest_days} days versus {baseline_days} overall.
problem_statements.population: All policies with a valid non-negative turnaround, grouped by product.
problem_statements.caveat: Turnaround differences may reflect product complexity rather than operational performance; the data cannot separate the two.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies with a valid non-negative turnaround, grouped by product.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Show me everything about a specific policy.
problem_statements.business_intent: Retrieve a single policy's full cross-table record.
problem_statements.business_objective: Assemble one policy's details from all tables it appears in.
example_queries: Give me the full record for this policy
analytical_steps: Validate the supplied AppID against Policy_Details.
Return the policy row.
Left join Owner_Details, Persistency_Details and Claims_Details on AppID.
Left join Sales_Details on SALES_ID for the selling agent.
Report which related records exist and which are absent, rather than presenting absence as a zero.
problem_statements.answer_template: Policy {app_id}: {plan_name}, status {status}, APE {ape}, sum assured {sum_assured}.
problem_statements.population: A single policy identified by AppID.
problem_statements.caveat: Owner name and postal code are personal data and are withheld by default. Absent related records mean no claim or no renewal row exists, not a zero value: a surrendered or death policy has no Persistency row at all, because Persistency covers only the active-or-lapsed eligible population (DQ-006).

evidence_requirements.population_definition: A single policy identified by AppID.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How many policies were issued each month?
problem_statements.business_intent: Track new-business volume over time.
problem_statements.business_objective: Produce a monthly time series of policies going in force.
analytical_steps: Parse Inforce.Date using the contract format list.
Derive a year-month period from the parsed date, not from Inforce.month.
Group by period and count policies and sum APE.
Order chronologically and report the series.
problem_statements.answer_template: Monthly issuance runs from {first_period} to {last_period}, peaking at {peak_count} in {peak_period}.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies, spanning January 2023 to December 2025.
problem_statements.caveat: The period is derived from Inforce.Date. The Inforce.month column is an unpadded YYYYM/YYYYMM integer that sorts incorrectly (DQ-010) and is not used.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies, spanning January 2023 to December 2025.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the premium trend over time?
problem_statements.business_intent: Track premium generation over time.
problem_statements.business_objective: Produce a monthly APE series and quantify the direction of travel.
analytical_steps: Derive the year-month period from Inforce.Date.
Sum APE and count policies per period.
Compute average APE per policy per period.
Compare the latest period and the latest quarter against earlier ones.
Report direction with the underlying volumes so a mix shift is visible.
problem_statements.answer_template: APE moved from {first_ape} in {first_period} to {last_ape} in {last_period}.
problem_statements.population: All policies with a parsed Inforce.Date.
problem_statements.caveat: A change in total APE can come from volume or from average case size; both are reported so the two are not confused. The extract ends in December 2025 and the final period may be partial.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies with a parsed Inforce.Date.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which branches write the most business?
problem_statements.business_intent: Identify the strongest branches.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank branches by policy volume and APE, with a sample guard.
analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by Branch_No.
Count policies and sum APE per branch.
Compute each branch share of the portfolio.
Rank by the requested measure and return the top N.
problem_statements.answer_template: {top_branch} leads with {top_count} policies and {top_ape} APE.
problem_statements.population: All policies across 5,719 branches.
problem_statements.caveat: The median branch has only 3 policies and the largest has 75, so most branch rates are small-sample. Branch_No is an opaque identifier with no name, region or hierarchy in the data.

limitations: no branch name or geography available
evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies across 5,719 branches.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the overall lapse rate?
problem_statements.business_intent: Establish the headline lapse measure.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute lapsed policies as a share of the book.
analytical_steps: Count policies with POLICY.STATUS = 'Lapsed'.
Divide by the total policy count.
Report the count and the percentage.
problem_statements.answer_template: {lapsed_count} of {policy_count} policies have lapsed, a rate of {lapse_rate}%.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details; 2,737 carry Lapsed status.
problem_statements.caveat: There is no lapse-date or lapse-reason column. Lapse is a status only, so it cannot be attributed to a period, a cause or a sequence of events.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details; 2,737 carry Lapsed status.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Does lapse rate vary by customer age?
problem_statements.business_intent: Find the age segments most prone to lapse.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute lapse rate by owner age band.

baseline.description: portfolio lapse rate across all policies

analytical_steps: Join Policy_Details to Owner_Details on AppID.
Band Owner.Age into decades.
Compute lapse rate per band with policy counts.
Compare each band against the portfolio lapse rate.
Flag bands with fewer than 100 policies.
problem_statements.answer_template: Lapse rate peaks at {worst_rate}% in the {worst_band} age band versus {baseline_rate}% overall.
problem_statements.population: The 24,999 policies that join to an owner record.
problem_statements.caveat: Owner.Age includes implausible values as low as 1 (DQ-009); ages below 18 are reported separately rather than banded with adults. One policy cannot be joined because of the corrupted AppID (DQ-001).

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 24,999 policies that join to an owner record.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Does lapse rate vary by customer occupation?
problem_statements.business_intent: Identify occupational segments with weak persistency.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute lapse rate by owner occupation.
example_queries: Do business owners lapse more than salaried?

baseline.description: portfolio lapse rate across all policies

analytical_steps: Join Policy_Details to Owner_Details on AppID.
Group by Owner.Occupation.
Compute lapse rate and policy count per occupation.
Compare each against the portfolio baseline.
Rank by lapse rate descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {worst_occupation} lapses at {worst_rate}% versus {baseline_rate}% overall.
problem_statements.population: The 24,999 joined policies across 6 occupation categories.
problem_statements.caveat: Occupation is self-declared at application and is not verified in the data.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 24,999 joined policies across 6 occupation categories.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Does lapse rate vary by customer income?
problem_statements.business_intent: Test whether affordability tracks with lapse.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute lapse rate by owner income band.
example_queries: Do lower income customers lapse more?

baseline.description: portfolio lapse rate across all policies

analytical_steps: Join Policy_Details to Owner_Details on AppID.
Band Owner.Earned.Income into ranges.
Compute lapse rate, policy count and average APE per band.
Report the premium-to-income relationship alongside the lapse rate.
Compare each band against the portfolio baseline.
problem_statements.answer_template: Lapse rate is highest at {worst_rate}% in the {worst_band} income band.
problem_statements.population: The 24,999 joined policies.
problem_statements.caveat: Owner.Earned.Income reaches 8,384,891,049, which is implausible (DQ-009). Extreme values are isolated into a top band rather than distorting the others. Income is declared at application and is not updated.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 24,999 joined policies.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which agents have the worst lapse rates?
problem_statements.business_intent: Identify agents whose business does not persist.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank agents by the lapse rate of the policies they sold, with a minimum sample guard.
example_queries: Which agents have the most lapses?

baseline.description: portfolio lapse rate across all policies

analytical_steps: Group Policy_Details by SALES_ID.
Compute lapse rate and policy count per agent.
Apply a minimum sample threshold, defaulting to 30 policies.
Join Sales_Details for the agent's recorded first-year persistency and active status.
Compare each agent against the portfolio lapse rate.
Rank by lapse rate descending and return the worst N.
problem_statements.answer_template: {worst_agent} has a {worst_rate}% lapse rate across {worst_count} policies versus {baseline_rate}% overall.
problem_statements.population: Agents with at least the minimum policy count. The median agent has only 8 policies; 242 of 1,956 agents have 30 or more.
problem_statements.caveat: Without the sample threshold, an agent with two policies and one lapse would rank at 50%. The threshold is applied and the excluded agent count is reported. A high lapse rate is an observation about the agent's book, not proof of misconduct.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: Agents with at least the minimum policy count. The median agent has only 8 policies; 242 of 1,956 agents have 30 or more.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is driving lapses across the portfolio?
problem_statements.business_intent: Explain portfolio lapse using every observable dimension.
problem_statements.business_objective: Scan all available attributes for the largest observable differences between lapsed and in-force policies.
example_queries: What factors are associated with lapse?
analytical_steps: Split policies into lapsed and premium-paying cohorts.
Join Owner_Details and Sales_Details to enrich both cohorts.
For every categorical attribute compute the lapse rate per level.
For every numeric attribute compute the mean and median in each cohort.
Compute the difference and percentage difference for each attribute.
Rank attributes by the size of the gap, reporting sample sizes alongside.
Present the strongest observable associations and state plainly that the data cannot establish which, if any, is causal.
problem_statements.answer_template: Portfolio lapse is {lapse_rate}%. The attributes differing most between lapsed and in-force policies are {top_drivers}. These are associations only.
problem_statements.population: All policies with status Lapsed or Premium paying (regular), joined to owner and agent.
problem_statements.caveat: The dataset has no lapse reason, no premium payment history, no customer contact log and no lapse date. Product and vintage are confounded with each other, so an apparent product effect may be a timing effect. No causal claim is supportable from this data.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies with status Lapsed or Premium paying (regular), joined to owner and agent.

limitations: Reports association only; causation is explicitly disclaimed.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How does lapse rate vary by policy vintage?
problem_statements.business_intent: See whether newer or older business persists better.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute lapse rate by in-force cohort period.

baseline.description: portfolio lapse rate across all policies

analytical_steps: Derive the in-force year from Inforce.Date.
Group policies into annual cohorts.
Compute lapse rate and policy count per cohort.
Report exposure duration per cohort so unequal maturity is visible.
Compare cohorts against each other rather than against a single baseline.
problem_statements.answer_template: The {worst_cohort} cohort lapses at {worst_rate}% against {best_rate}% for {best_cohort}.
problem_statements.population: All policies, grouped by year of Inforce.Date (2023-2025).
problem_statements.caveat: Cohorts have unequal exposure: 2023 business has had up to three years to lapse while 2025 business has had months. Rates are therefore not directly comparable, and this is stated rather than adjusted, because There is no lapse-date or lapse-reason column. Lapse is a status only, so it cannot be attributed to a period, a cause or a sequence of events.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All policies, grouped by year of Inforce.Date (2023-2025).

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the surrender rate and which products drive it?
problem_statements.business_intent: Quantify voluntary exits and locate them.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute the surrender rate overall and by product.
analytical_steps: Count policies with POLICY.STATUS = 'Surrendered' and compute the portfolio rate.
Group by product and compute the surrender rate per product.
Sum the APE attached to surrendered policies as the value lost.
Flag low-sample products and rank the rest.
problem_statements.answer_template: {surrendered_count} policies surrendered ({surrender_rate}%), concentrated in {top_product}.
problem_statements.population: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details; 324 carry Surrendered status.
problem_statements.caveat: The data holds no surrender date, surrender value, surrender charge or surrender reason. Only the status and the policy's own attributes are observable, so the economics of surrender cannot be analysed.

limitations: no surrender date, value or reason available
evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 25,000 policies in Policy_Details; 324 carry Surrendered status.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How do surrendered policies differ from those still in force?
problem_statements.business_intent: Profile the surrendering customer.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compare surrendered and in-force cohorts across every observable attribute.
example_queries: What do surrendering customers look like?
analytical_steps: Select surrendered policies and premium-paying policies as two cohorts.
Join Owner_Details to both.
Compute the mean and median of each numeric attribute per cohort.
Compute the distribution of each categorical attribute per cohort.
Report the largest differences with sample sizes.
problem_statements.answer_template: Surrendered policies average {surr_ape} APE versus {inforce_ape} for in-force policies.
problem_statements.population: 324 surrendered policies versus 21,805 premium-paying policies.
problem_statements.caveat: The surrendered cohort is small (324 policies), so segment breakdowns within it are fragile and minimum cell sizes are enforced. Differences are associations, not reasons for surrender.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: 324 surrendered policies versus 21,805 premium-paying policies.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the overall renewal payment rate?
problem_statements.business_intent: Establish the headline renewal collection measure.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute the share of renewals recorded as paid.
example_queries: How many renewals have been paid?
analytical_steps: Count rows with Renewal_Status = 'Paid'.
Divide by the total persistency row count.
Report paid and pending counts and rates.
problem_statements.answer_template: {paid_count} of {renewal_count} renewals are paid, a rate of {renewal_paid_rate}%.
problem_statements.population: Persistency_Details covers only Premium paying (regular) and Lapsed policies. Surrendered and death policies have no renewal row (DQ-006), so this denominator differs from the full policy count.
problem_statements.caveat: 'Pending' means not yet recorded as paid at extract time, not necessarily defaulted. Renewal_Status = 'Paid' is exactly equivalent to a present Renewal_Paid_Date, so the two agree by construction.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: Persistency_Details covers only Premium paying (regular) and Lapsed policies. Surrendered and death policies have no renewal row (DQ-006), so this denominator differs from the full policy count.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How does persistency differ across the 13th, 25th and 37th month buckets?
problem_statements.business_intent: Track how retention decays with policy age.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compare renewal paid rates across the three persistency buckets.
analytical_steps: Group Persistency_Details by Persistency_Bucket.
Compute the renewal paid rate and row count per bucket.
Sum the renewal premium at stake per bucket.
Order the buckets chronologically (13th, 25th, 37th) rather than alphabetically.
Report the trajectory across buckets.
problem_statements.answer_template: Renewal paid rate runs {b13}% at the 13th month, {b25}% at the 25th and {b37}% at the 37th.
problem_statements.population: Persistency_Details covers only Premium paying (regular) and Lapsed policies. Surrendered and death policies have no renewal row (DQ-006), so this denominator differs from the full policy count. 6,943 / 8,189 / 9,410 rows per bucket.
problem_statements.caveat: Each policy appears in exactly one bucket, so these are three different populations, not the same cohort tracked over time. A decay reading across buckets is therefore a cross-sectional comparison, not a longitudinal one.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: Persistency_Details covers only Premium paying (regular) and Lapsed policies. Surrendered and death policies have no renewal row (DQ-006), so this denominator differs from the full policy count. 6,943 / 8,189 / 9,410 rows per bucket.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How late are customers paying their renewals?
problem_statements.business_intent: Understand payment timing behaviour.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute the delay between renewal due date and renewal paid date.
analytical_steps: Restrict to rows where Renewal_Paid_Date is present.
Derive renewal_delay_days as paid date minus due date.
Compute the distribution: minimum, median, maximum and percentiles.
Count how many were paid on or before the due date versus after.
Report the delay distribution.
problem_statements.answer_template: Of {paid_count} paid renewals, the median delay is {median_delay} days and {late_count} were paid after the due date.
problem_statements.population: The 12,439 persistency rows with a recorded Renewal_Paid_Date.
problem_statements.caveat: Pending renewals have no paid date and are excluded from the delay distribution rather than counted as zero or infinite delay. Observed delays span 0 to 20 days, so this measures grace-period behaviour, not default.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: paid renewals only

problem_statements.problem_statement: Does payment method affect renewal behaviour?
problem_statements.business_intent: See whether auto-debit or digital methods improve collection.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compare renewal paid rate and delay across payment modes.
analytical_steps: Group Persistency_Details by Payment_Mode.
Compute the renewal paid rate per mode.
Compute the median payment delay per mode for paid rows.
Compare each mode against the overall rate.
Rank modes by paid rate.
problem_statements.answer_template: {best_mode} has the highest paid rate at {best_rate}% versus {baseline_rate}% overall.
problem_statements.population: Persistency_Details covers only Premium paying (regular) and Lapsed policies. Surrendered and death policies have no renewal row (DQ-006), so this denominator differs from the full policy count. Five payment modes, each with roughly 4,800-5,000 rows.
problem_statements.caveat: Payment mode is recorded on the renewal row, not chosen at policy level. Policy.Mode is single-valued ('Annually') and is unrelated to this field. Any difference is an association; customers are not randomly assigned a mode.

aggregates: paid rate and delay by mode
evidence_requirements.population_definition: Persistency_Details covers only Premium paying (regular) and Lapsed policies. Surrendered and death policies have no renewal row (DQ-006), so this denominator differs from the full policy count. Five payment modes, each with roughly 4,800-5,000 rows.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How much renewal premium is still outstanding?
problem_statements.business_intent: Size the collection opportunity and the value at risk.
problem_statements.business_objective: Total the renewal premium attached to pending renewals.
example_queries: How much renewal premium is pending?
Value at risk from unpaid renewals
analytical_steps: Filter Persistency_Details to Renewal_Status = 'Pending'.
Sum Renewal_Premium_Amount across those rows.
Break the total down by persistency bucket.
Express the pending amount as a share of total renewal premium due.
Report counts alongside values.
problem_statements.answer_template: {pending_count} renewals worth {pending_premium} are outstanding, {pending_share}% of renewal premium due.
problem_statements.population: The 12,103 persistency rows with Renewal_Status = 'Pending'.
problem_statements.caveat: Pending means not recorded as paid at extract time. The data has no grace period, no lapse date and no collection activity, so pending cannot be equated with lost premium.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 12,103 persistency rows with Renewal_Status = 'Pending'.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which agents have the best renewal collection?
problem_statements.business_intent: Identify agents whose customers keep paying.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank agents by the renewal paid rate of their book, with a sample guard.
analytical_steps: Group Persistency_Details by SALES_ID.
Compute the renewal paid rate and row count per agent.
Apply the minimum sample threshold.
Join Sales_Details to bring in the recorded first-year persistency rate.
Compare the computed rate against the recorded rate and report both.
Rank by computed paid rate descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {best_agent} collects {best_rate}% of renewals across {best_count} policies.
problem_statements.population: Agents present in Persistency_Details with at least the minimum row count (1,955 agents in total).
problem_statements.caveat: Sales_Details.First Year Persistency Rate is a supplied agent-level figure covering a different measurement basis from the renewal paid rate computed here; they are reported side by side and are not expected to match. That column is null for 369 agents (DQ-005).

limitations: two different persistency bases reported side by side
evidence_requirements.population_definition: Agents present in Persistency_Details with at least the minimum row count (1,955 agents in total).

problem_statements.problem_statement: Why is renewal collection weakest in the 37th month bucket?
problem_statements.business_intent: Explain the weakest persistency bucket with observable evidence.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compare the weakest bucket against the others across every available attribute.
example_queries: What is wrong with the 37th month bucket?
Why do older policies stop paying?
analytical_steps: Identify the bucket with the lowest renewal paid rate.
Join Policy_Details and Owner_Details onto the persistency rows.
Profile the weak bucket and the other buckets across product mix, premium size, payment mode, policy status, owner age, income and occupation.
Compute the gap for each attribute and rank by gap size.
Check whether the weak bucket contains a different product or status mix, which would make the comparison a mix effect rather than a timing effect.
Report observable differences and state what cannot be concluded.
problem_statements.answer_template: The {weak_bucket} bucket collects {weak_rate}% versus {other_rate}% elsewhere. The largest observable differences are {top_drivers}, which are associations, not causes.
problem_statements.population: All persistency rows, grouped by bucket and joined to policy and owner.
problem_statements.caveat: Buckets are different populations, not one cohort over time, so an apparent decay may be a composition difference. The data holds no payment history, no customer contact record and no reason code, so the mechanism cannot be established.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All persistency rows, grouped by bucket and joined to policy and owner.

limitations: Association only; bucket differences may be composition, not timing.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What is the renewal paid rate by product?
problem_statements.business_intent: Find which products retain paying customers.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute renewal paid rate per product over the eligible population.
analytical_steps: Join Persistency_Details to Policy_Details on AppID.
Group by product.
Compute the renewal paid rate and row count per product.
Compute the renewal premium outstanding per product.
Compare against the overall paid rate and rank.
problem_statements.answer_template: {best_product} renews at {best_rate}% against an overall {baseline_rate}%.
problem_statements.population: The 24,541 policies present in both Policy_Details and Persistency_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: Persistency_Details covers only Premium paying (regular) and Lapsed policies. Surrendered and death policies have no renewal row (DQ-006), so this denominator differs from the full policy count. Surrendered and death policies are excluded, so a product losing customers through surrender rather than non-renewal will look better here than it is.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 24,541 policies present in both Policy_Details and Persistency_Details.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How many claims have been made and what is their total value?
problem_statements.business_intent: Establish the headline claims position.
problem_statements.business_objective: Report claim volume, total claimed and total paid.
example_queries: How many claims do we have?
What have we paid out in claims?
analytical_steps: Count rows in Claims_Details.
Sum Claim.Amount, stripping thousands separators before coercion.
Sum Amount.Paid over settled claims only.
Report volume, claimed total and paid total.
problem_statements.answer_template: {claim_count} claims totalling {total_claim_amount} claimed, {total_amount_paid} paid.
problem_statements.population: All 134 claims. Every claim in Claims_Details corresponds to a policy with POLICY.STATUS = 'Death'. There is no claim-type column, no maturity, surrender, health or rider claim, so all claim analysis is death-claim analysis.
problem_statements.caveat: One claim is unsettled and carries the literal 'WIP' in Status.of.Claim, Amount.Paid and Settlement.Date (DQ-004). It is excluded from settlement and payout metrics and the exclusion is reported. Claim amounts use Indian lakh grouping and must be parsed with separator stripping (DQ-003).

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 134 claims. Every claim in Claims_Details corresponds to a policy with POLICY.STATUS = 'Death'. There is no claim-type column, no maturity, surrender, health or rider claim, so all claim analysis is death-claim analysis.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What are the leading causes of death in our claims?
problem_statements.business_intent: Understand mortality drivers in the claimed book.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank causes of death by claim count and value.
analytical_steps: Group Claims_Details by Cause.of.Death.
Count claims and sum claim amount per cause.
Compute each cause share of total claims.
Rank by count descending.
problem_statements.answer_template: {top_cause} is the leading cause with {top_count} claims ({top_share}%).
problem_statements.population: All 134 claims across 45 distinct cause values.
problem_statements.caveat: Cause.of.Death is free text with 45 distinct values across 134 claims, including near-duplicates such as 'NATURAL DEATH' and 'NATURAL'. It is not a coded taxonomy, so grouping is by literal value and similar causes are not merged. The field records the cause attributed at claim stage; it is not evidence of a mortality driver in the wider book and cannot establish any causal relationship with product, agent or customer attributes. The book contains 134 claims against 25,000 policies. Any breakdown of claims by a dimension produces small cells, so counts are reported alongside every rate and minimum cell sizes are enforced.

limitations: free-text cause, not a coded taxonomy
evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 134 claims across 45 distinct cause values.

problem_statements.problem_statement: What proportion of claims have been settled?
problem_statements.business_intent: Measure claims processing completion.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute the settled share of claims.
example_queries: How many claims are still open?
What percentage of claims are paid?
analytical_steps: Count claims with Status.of.Claim = 'Paid'.
Count claims with any other status.
Compute the settled share.
problem_statements.answer_template: {paid_count} of {claim_count} claims are settled, a rate of {settlement_rate}%.
problem_statements.population: All 134 claims in Claims_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: Status.of.Claim has exactly two values, 'Paid' and 'WIP'. There is no repudiated, rejected or contested status in the data, so claim-decision analysis is not possible.

limitations: no repudiation or rejection status exists
evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 134 claims in Claims_Details.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Do we pay claims in full?
problem_statements.business_intent: Check whether settled amounts match amounts claimed.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute the payout ratio and identify claims settled above or below the claimed amount.
example_queries: Do we pay the full claim amount?
analytical_steps: Restrict to settled claims, excluding the WIP row.
Parse both money columns with thousands-separator stripping.
Derive payout_ratio as Amount.Paid divided by Claim.Amount.
Count claims paid exactly, below and above the claimed amount.
Report the aggregate payout ratio and the exceptions.
problem_statements.answer_template: {exact_count} of {settled_count} settled claims paid exactly as claimed; {under_count} paid less and {over_count} more.
problem_statements.population: The 133 settled claims. One claim is unsettled and carries the literal 'WIP' in Status.of.Claim, Amount.Paid and Settlement.Date (DQ-004). It is excluded from settlement and payout metrics and the exclusion is reported.
problem_statements.caveat: The data holds no deduction, rider, interest or ex-gratia column, so a difference between claimed and paid cannot be explained from the CSVs. Differences are reported as observations, not as errors.

evidence_requirements.records: claims where paid differs from claimed
limitations: no explanation column for payment differences
evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 133 settled claims. One claim is unsettled and carries the literal 'WIP' in Status.of.Claim, Amount.Paid and Settlement.Date (DQ-004). It is excluded from settlement and payout metrics and the exclusion is reported.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How long does it take to intimate and settle a claim?
problem_statements.business_intent: Measure claims service turnaround.
problem_statements.business_objective: Compute intimation lag and settlement lag distributions.
analytical_steps: Parse the three claim date columns using the contract's format list, which covers both '%d-%b-%y' and the few '%m/%d/%Y' values.
Derive intimation_lag_days as intimation minus death.
Derive settlement_lag_days as settlement minus intimation.
Exclude the unsettled claim from settlement-lag statistics.
Report median, mean and the tail percentiles for each lag.
problem_statements.answer_template: Median intimation lag is {median_intimation} days; median settlement lag is {median_settlement} days.
problem_statements.population: All 134 claims for intimation lag; the 133 settled claims for settlement lag.
problem_statements.caveat: One claim is unsettled and carries the literal 'WIP' in Status.of.Claim, Amount.Paid and Settlement.Date (DQ-004). It is excluded from settlement and payout metrics and the exclusion is reported. Intimation lag reaches 483 days in the tail, so the median is reported as the representative figure rather than the mean.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 134 claims for intimation lag; the 133 settled claims for settlement lag.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which claims took longest to settle and why?
problem_statements.business_intent: Understand what distinguishes slow claims.
problem_statements.business_objective: Identify the slowest-settling claims and compare them against fast ones on every observable attribute.
example_queries: Why do some claims take longer?
analytical_steps: Derive settlement lag for every settled claim.
Split claims into the slowest quartile and the rest.
Join Policy_Details and Owner_Details for context.
Compare claim amount, sum assured, cause of death, intimation lag, policy tenure at death and owner age across the two groups.
Rank attributes by the size of the observable gap.
Report only what the data shows and state the limits explicitly.
problem_statements.answer_template: The slowest quartile settles in {slow_median} days versus {fast_median} days. The largest observable differences are {top_drivers}, which are associations, not causes.
problem_statements.population: The 133 settled claims, split into the slowest quartile and the remainder.
problem_statements.caveat: With 133 settled claims a quartile holds roughly 33 cases, so differences are fragile and confidence is low. The data has no investigation flag, no document or query log and no claim-handler field, so the actual reason for delay is not observable. The book contains 134 claims against 25,000 policies. Any breakdown of claims by a dimension produces small cells, so counts are reported alongside every rate and minimum cell sizes are enforced.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 133 settled claims, split into the slowest quartile and the remainder.

limitations: Sample of 133 claims; associations only, no causal claim.

problem_statements.problem_statement: How many deaths occurred soon after the policy went in force?
problem_statements.business_intent: Surface early-claim exposure, a classic anti-selection signal.
problem_statements.business_objective: Count and profile claims where death occurred within a short window of inforce.

analytical_steps: Join Claims_Details to Policy_Details on AppID.
Parse both date columns under the contract's format rules.
Derive days_from_inforce_to_death.
Filter to claims within the configured early-claim window, default 365 days.
Count them, sum their value and profile them by product and agent.
Report the early-claim share of all claims.
problem_statements.answer_template: {early_count} of {claim_count} claims occurred within {window_days} days of inforce, worth {early_value}.
problem_statements.population: All 134 claims joined to their policy; every claim joins successfully.
problem_statements.caveat: The observed minimum is 15 days from inforce to death and 58 claims fall within 365 days. Early death is not evidence of fraud or misrepresentation; the data holds no underwriting, medical or investigation field to assess that. Sales_Details carries an agent-level Early Claim Rate on a different basis.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 134 claims joined to their policy; every claim joins successfully.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which products carry the highest claim incidence?

Group by product.
Count claims and policies per product and compute incidence.
Compare against the portfolio incidence rate.
Flag products whose claim count is below the minimum cell size.

With 134 claims across 10 products, several products have fewer than 10 claims and their rates are not stable. Compare product mix, average case size, customer age, customer income, geography, payment mode and renewal behaviour against the peer benchmark.

Rank attributes by gap size to surface the strongest observable differences.
State which differences the data supports and which explanations it cannot establish, including anything about the agent's own behaviour.

problem_statements.caveat: Every difference reported here is an association, not a proven cause: the data cannot establish why this agent outperforms. There is no agent name, tenure, geography, hierarchy, channel or target, so agent performance cannot be explained by agent characteristics.). aggregates: book profile for agent and peers

Compute the agent's metrics from their own policy and persistency rows.
Compute the same metrics across all eligible peers as the benchmark.
Compute the agent's rank and percentile on each metric.
Present a side-by-side table with the gap on every metric.
problem_statements.answer_template: Agent {agent_id}: {policy_count} policies, {lapse_rate}% lapse versus {peer_lapse}% peer average (rank {rank_position}).

The median agent has 8 policies and only 242 of 1,956 agents have 30 or more. Any agent rate computed from their own book needs a minimum sample threshold, which is applied and whose excluded count is reported. The renewal paid rate is computed over the Persistency-eligible population only, which excludes the agent's surrendered and death policies (DQ-006), so it uses a smaller denominator than the lapse rate.

Share of book from top agents
How dependent are we on top agents?

Sort agents by contribution descending and compute cumulative share.
Determine the share held by the top 1%, 5%, 10% and 20% of agents.
Compute a Herfindahl-style index over agent shares.
Report both the volume and the APE concentration curves.
problem_statements.answer_template: The top 10% of agents write {top10_share}% of policies and {top10_ape_share}% of APE.
problem_statements.population: All 1,956 agents and 25,000 policies.
problem_statements.caveat: Agent production ranges from 1 to 151 policies with a median of 8, so concentration is substantial by construction. There is no agent hierarchy or team structure in the data, so this measures individual, not team, concentration.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 1,956 agents and 25,000 policies.

Join Policy_Details to compute production per agent.
Compute mean and median of each quality rate per group.
Compute the lapse rate of each group's policies.
Present a side-by-side comparison with group sizes.
problem_statements.answer_template: Active agents ({active_count}) average {active_ape} APE; inactive agents ({inactive_count}) average {inactive_ape}.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Which agents raise the most conduct concerns?
problem_statements.business_intent: Surface agents whose selling practice generates complaints and rejections.
problem_statements.business_objective: Rank agents on the supplied conduct-risk rates.

Apply the minimum policy threshold.
Rank agents on the requested conduct metric.
Compute the population mean as the baseline.
Return the top N with all conduct rates shown side by side.
problem_statements.answer_template: {worst_agent} records a {worst_rate} {metric} against a population average of {baseline_rate}.
problem_statements.population: Agents meeting the minimum policy threshold.
problem_statements.caveat: These are supplied rates whose definition, denominator and window are not documented (Sales_Details holds supplied agent-level rates with no stated definition, denominator or measurement window. They are used as recorded and are never silently reconciled against rates computed from Policy_Details.). A high rate is an indicator warranting review, not a finding of misconduct. evidence_requirements.population_definition: Agents meeting the minimum policy threshold.

analytical_steps: Restrict to agents meeting the minimum policy threshold.
Join Policy_Details to Sales_Details on SALES_ID and left join Persistency_Details on AppID to assemble each agent's book.
Collect the seven supplied conduct and persistency rates per agent.
Compute the agent's observed lapse rate and renewal paid rate from their own book.
Convert every component to a percentile rank within the eligible population, so components on different scales become comparable.
Orient every component so that a higher percentile always means better.
Combine with declared, inspectable weights into a composite score.
Report the composite alongside every component so the score is auditable.
Flag agents with a null first-year persistency rate as scored on fewer components.
problem_statements.answer_template: Composite quality scores computed for {scored_agents} agents; {best_agent} ranks first and {worst_agent} last.
problem_statements.population: Agents meeting the minimum policy threshold and present in Sales_Details.
problem_statements.caveat: The weights are a declared analytical convention, not a company standard; they are stored in config and shown with the result so the score can be challenged and recomputed. Percentile ranking is used because the seven supplied rates sit on different and undocumented scales, with maxima ranging from 1.28 to 25.96. 369 agents lack a persistency rate (DQ-005) and are scored on the remaining components, which is stated on their row.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: Agents meeting the minimum policy threshold and present in Sales_Details.

limitations: Composite depends on declared weights; not an official company rating.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Do agents with poor conduct indicators also produce more lapses?

Rank agents into quartiles on the chosen conduct metric.
Join Policy_Details to Sales_Details on SALES_ID and left join Persistency_Details on AppID to pool each quartile's underlying book.
For each quartile pool the underlying policies.
Compute the observed lapse rate and renewal paid rate for each quartile's pooled book.
Compare the worst quartile against the best and report the gap with counts.
State that a monotonic pattern across quartiles is suggestive but not proof.

problem_statements.caveat: This is an association between two measures over the same agents; it cannot establish that conduct causes lapse, nor rule out that both reflect a shared cause such as customer segment or territory. Neither is observable in the data. Sales_Details holds supplied agent-level rates with no stated definition, denominator or measurement window. They are used as recorded and are never silently reconciled against rates computed from Policy_Details. The renewal paid rate covers only the Persistency-eligible population, which excludes surrendered and death policies (DQ-006), so it rests on a smaller denominator than the lapse rate computed beside it.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: Agents above the sample threshold, pooled into conduct quartiles.

Join Policy_Details to Sales_Details on SALES_ID to establish each agent's book size.
For each supplied rate compute the population median and interquartile range.
Flag agents beyond 1.5 times the IQR above the third quartile.
Record which metrics each flagged agent breaches and by how much.
Rank flagged agents by the number of metrics breached, then by severity.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: Agents above the minimum policy threshold with non-null rates.

problem_statements.problem_statement: Where should we focus agent remediation effort?

analytical_steps: Restrict to Active agents meeting the minimum policy threshold.
Join Policy_Details to Sales_Details on SALES_ID and left join Persistency_Details on AppID to assemble each agent's exposure.

Compute each agent's observed lapse rate and pending renewal premium.
Combine risk level with exposure, so a weak agent with a large book outranks an equally weak agent with a small one.

The data supports identifying where to look; it cannot recommend a specific intervention, because no record of past interventions or their outcomes exists. Sales_Details holds supplied agent-level rates with no stated definition, denominator or measurement window. They are used as recorded and are never silently reconciled against rates computed from Policy_Details.

limitations: no intervention history to recommend a specific action

problem_statements.problem_statement: How does declared income relate to the premium customers pay?

problem_statements.business_objective: Compare APE against declared income across income bands.
example_queries: Do richer customers pay more premium?
analytical_steps: Join Owner_Details to Policy_Details on AppID.
Band Owner.Earned.Income, isolating zero and implausibly large values.
Compute median APE and median sum assured per band.
Compute the premium-to-income ratio per band as an affordability indicator.
Report the pattern across bands with counts.
problem_statements.answer_template: Median APE rises from {low_ape} in the lowest income band to {high_ape} in the highest.
problem_statements.population: The 24,999 joined records with a declared income.
problem_statements.caveat: Declared income has 451 distinct values across 25,000 records with a maximum of 8,384,891,049 and a minimum of zero, which suggests banding at entry and at least some placeholder values. The premium-to-income ratio is therefore indicative only and is not a suitability assessment. Owner attributes are declared at application and are not verified or updated. Owner.Age includes values as low as 1 and Owner.Earned.Income reaches 8,384,891,049 (DQ-009), so medians are reported alongside means and implausible values are isolated rather than dropped.

limitations: income appears banded and contains placeholders
evidence_requirements.population_definition: The 24,999 joined records with a declared income.

Group by ClientID and count distinct policies.
Filter to clients holding more than one policy.
Sum their combined APE and compute their lapse rate.
Compare multi-policy clients against single-policy clients.
problem_statements.answer_template: {multi_count} clients hold more than one policy, contributing {multi_ape} in combined APE.
problem_statements.population: All 24,757 distinct clients; 237 hold more than one policy, at most 3.

evidence_requirements.population_definition: All 24,757 distinct clients; 237 hold more than one policy, at most 3.

Rank clients by total APE and split into value tiers by percentile.
Left join Persistency_Details to compute each tier's renewal paid rate.
Profile each tier on age, income, occupation, education, product mix and geography.

Present the tiers with the concentration of value made explicit.

Select the two most recent complete periods, or the two the user names.

For each cohort compute status mix, average case size and renewal paid rate.
Report the elapsed exposure of each cohort alongside its rates.
Compare cohorts, making unequal maturity explicit.
